messages.body_plain:
Hi there

I have recently installed R from cran-lenny backport site; the version I
have for R is 2.9.2. I have updated, from inside R itself, all my
packages, and I have install.package()'d ggplot2.

When I try to follow some examples from ggplot website, the following
errors are issued:

 > library(ggplot2)
Loading required package: proto
Loading required package: grid
Loading required package: reshape
Loading required package: plyr

Attaching package: 'ggplot2'

         The following object(s) are masked from package:grid :

          nullGrob

 > ggmissing(french_fries)
 > ffm <- melt(french_fries, id = 1:4, preserve.na <http://preserve.na> = FALSE)

   unused argument(s) (data$value[0])

messages.subject: Re: beanplots, axis, censored data
messages.body_plain:
On Oct 26, 2:08 pm, Harlan Harris <harlan.har...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Welcome to R!
>
> > 1) Beanplots - I'm guessing that it's possible to reproduce these
> > plots using ggplot2, but I've no clue as to how.  Has anybody
> > attempted it?
>
> A what? (google, google) Oh, interesting. Sorta like a violin plot
> with really wide rug lines down the middle. There's a beanplot package
> for R. No, I don't think anyone's ported it to ggplot2. Depending on
> whether the beanplot package separates the computations from the
> graphical code, it might not be hard to use its calculations in
> combination with stat_summary to generate the plot, at least the
> single-variable version.

We discovered this type of plot quite recently and like it a lot.  We
find it useful to see the distribution as well as the number of
samples that cause this distribution to occur. From the description, a
bean consists of a one dimensional scatter plot, its distribution as a
density shape, and an average line for the distribution.  One can do
the violin plot in ggplot2, strip plots are possible too, but the
question is how to combine the two in one.  My other option is to
cheat and use the package as provided, but change the formatting to
look like a ggplot2 (because they are visually pleasing and to keep a
report looking consistent throughout).  Of course, the next problem
becomes a question of how to do that. ggplot2 uses mm for font size
compared to the cex of R, for example...

>
> > 2) 2nd x axis.  I understand and accept the limitation on 2nd axes as
> > enforced by ggplot2, but I am curious as to whether the location of
> > the x axis can be changed.  I would like to plot how concentrations of
> > contaminants changes down a soil profile and it makes more sense (as
> > well as commonly accepted) to have an x axis on the top rather than
> > the bottom.  Can this be done?
>
> I don't think so.

I have my depth data running from 0 to - 5 m.  This is acceptable
enough.

>
> > 3) Censored data:  How does one deal with this in ggplot2?  I've been
> > using the NADA package which does a pretty good job, but I prefer the
> > aesthetics of ggplot2.
>
> What would you like ggplot2 to do? The data doesn't know it's
> censored, so you have to tell ggplot to do something different. You
> could use the subset option to plot the points that are at the
> censoring boundaries differently somehow, perhaps using a different
> geom.

That is a good question.  Should have been more clear.  After having a
second and third look at the documentation and "Guidelines  for
computing summary statistics for data-sets containing non-detects"
2009, Huston and Juarez-Colunga, a handy pdf, I am confused as to how
approach this problem.  Essentially, I am after two things:
1) Creating boxplots (okay, to be perfectly honest, beanplots, but
I'll live with the beanplots given my limitations) based on censored
data. According to their description on p. 28, a boxplot for censored
data is the same as one for uncensored data, except there is a line at
the maximum censoring limit.   Easy enough to replicate, but they go
on show the limitations of substituting methods for censored data (p.
46) where they have a 0, 0.5CL, and a CL for substitutions, followed
by a "correct" boxplot.  Can't figure out what method they used for
the "correct" boxplot, but I'm guessing that it uses a Kaplan-Meier or
the like to produce a plot....
2) Scatterplots where the censored data is represented visually.
Actually, not that hard to do...
>
>  -Harlan

Thanks again for the responses!

Cheers,
Michael Hopgood
Environmental Consultant, MRM Konsult AB, Sweden.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to make a plot using qplot() which has a categorical
variable plotted on the y-axis, but I want the levels to be in a
specific order.  The first approach I tried was to code the y vector
as integer values, which allowed me to order the different levels, but
now I'd like to rename the ticks as the names of the categorical
variables instead of the integers.  A second approach would be to code
the y vector as text strings representing the levels of the
categorical variable, and then find a way to put these text strings in
an order other than alphabetical order.

Does anyone know how I can do this?

Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: Plotting a categorical variable using qplot()
messages.subject_clean: Plotting a categorical variable using qplot()
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Do you mean something like this?

d = data.frame(x=1:10,y=factor(sample(1:3,10,rep=T), labels=letters[1:3]))
str(d) # levels(y) in alphabetical order

qplot(x, y, data=d),
qplot(x,y, data=transform(d, y = relevel(y, "c"))),
qplot(x,y, data=transform(d, y = factor(y, levels=rev(letters[1:3]))))

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Nov 2, 2009 at 9:17 AM, baptiste auguie <bapt...@googlemail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> Do you mean something like this?
>
> d = data.frame(x=1:10,y=factor(sample(1:3,10,rep=T), labels=letters[1:3]))
> str(d) # levels(y) in alphabetical order
>
> qplot(x, y, data=d),
> qplot(x,y, data=transform(d, y = relevel(y, "c"))),
> qplot(x,y, data=transform(d, y = factor(y, levels=rev(letters[1:3]))))

Or

qplot(x, relevel(y, "c"), data = d)
qplot(x, factor(y, levels = rev(levels(y)), data = d)

Or to reorder based on some variable in the data:

qplot(reorder(y, x), x, data = d)

Hadley

messages.subject: possible bug in hline when combined with coord_flip()
messages.subject_clean: possible bug in hline when combined with coord_flip()
messages.body_plain:
Simple test case:

Straight plot:
ggplot(data.frame(a=1:10, b=1:5), aes(x=a, y=b)) + geom_point() +
geom_hline(aes(yintercept=3))

flipped plot:

ggplot(data.frame(a=1:10, b=1:5), aes(x=a, y=b)) + geom_point() +
geom_hline(aes(yintercept=3)) + coord_flip()

in the flipped plot the line does not extend to the whole figure as in
the un-flipped plot.
Alex

the 20 and 21 back to X and Y.

messages.subject_clean: Highlighing a subset of the data - combining plots
messages.body_plain:
How would you want the plots to be combined? In your example you use
different geoms (bin2d for the whole data and point for the subset),
do you want the bin2d with the points on top?
If yes use something like this:
qplot(carat, price, data=diamonds, geom="bin2d") + geom_point
(data=diamonds[100:200,])
or
ggplot(mapping=aes(x=carat, y=price)) +
    layer(data=diamonds, geom="bin2d") +
    layer(data=diamonds[100:200,], geom="point")

Of course it looks ugly with these datasets, but maybe it's useful
with your data.

messages.subject: Re: Still struggling with annotating different facet plots
messages.subject_clean: Still struggling with annotating different facet plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daren,

Create a data frame that indicates where each label should go:

examp <- data.frame(
  X=rnorm(20),
  Y=rnorm(20),
  fact=rep(c("a","b"),each=10)
)

corr <- ddply(examp, "fact", summarise, cor = cor(X, Y))

ggplot(examp,aes(X,Y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm") +
  geom_text(aes(1, 1, label = format(cor)), data = corr) +
  facet_grid(fact~.)

Hadley

Thanks a lot in advance. I really hope that there is a solution to this problem as these are (hopefully) the last problems from using ggplot "in production".

messages.subject: Re: panel size
messages.body_plain:
As an illustration of what I said earlier, the following creates two
separate plots that have the same width. You can also resize the
window in interactive use, the panel width remains constant. I added a
test with a grid.rect() of fixed width for comparison. I didn't
consider the plot margins, nor the height.

source("http://ggextra.googlecode.com/svn/trunk/inst/tests/fixedSize.r")

p1 <- qplot(1,1000, colour="test", linetype="longer legend") +
  ylab("double\nline")
p2 <- qplot(1,1, colour="test") +
  ylab("y")

test.rect <- function()
  grid.rect(width=unit(5, "cm") - unit(3, "lines"),
            gp=gpar(lty=2, col="red", fill="grey90"))

test <- opts(panel.background = test.rect)

g1 <- fixedsize(p1 + test, unit(5, "cm"))
g2 <- fixedsize(p2 + test, unit(5, "cm"))

pdf("test.pdf")
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(g1)
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(g2)
dev.off()

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Right, I think where you're getting hung up, Mattias, is a not-
completely-obvious aspect of how the "+" operator works. When you
build a ggplot out of a series of calls, what you're actually doing is
creating a single ggplot object that contains a variety of layers.
Each plot can only have a single base object, but any number of
layers. The geom_ and stat_ functions implicitly are adding layers to
the base plot. When you do qplot() + qplot(), you're trying to add a
plot to a plot, which doesn't really make sense, but what you want to
do, I think, is add a layer to a plot. So, Xavier's suggestions are
correct.

I would also add that the "right" way to do this is not to have two
dataframes, but instead to have a column in your single data frame
that flags interesting vs noninteresting cases. Then you can do
something like "+ geom_point(subset=blahblah, color="red")" to overlay
red dots on the interesting points.

I would further add that summary() of a ggplot object can be helpful
to see the layers that are generated by your calls. In the future,
there will likely be a more comprehensive and useful function to do
this... (work in progress...)

 -Harlan

On Nov 3, 11:14 am, Xavier <char...@agroparistech.fr> wrote:
> How would you want the plots to be combined? In your example you use
> different geoms (bin2d for the whole data and point for the subset),
> do you want the bin2d with the points on top?
> If yes use something like this:
> qplot(carat, price, data=diamonds, geom="bin2d") + geom_point
> (data=diamonds[100:200,])
> or
> ggplot(mapping=aes(x=carat, y=price)) +
>     layer(data=diamonds, geom="bin2d") +
>     layer(data=diamonds[100:200,], geom="point")
>
> Of course it looks ugly with these datasets, but maybe it's useful
> with your data.

Hi Matthias:
If you are trying to plot one dataframe and overlay a second dataframe to the same plot then the short example below should give you an idea on how to do it.

library(ggplot2)
     a <- data.frame(x=rnorm(1:10),y=rnorm(1:10),Z=rep(1,10));a
     b <- data.frame(x=runif(1:10),y=runif(1:10),Z=rep(2,10));b
     p <- qplot(x,y,data=a,geom="line");p
     # add second dataframe to the plot
     p %+% b

I would like to know what the best way to get around the quirk that
formulas with LHS (y) transformations are not being reverse translated
to the correct plotting space.  The example code at the bottom should
make it clear what I mean.

My end goal is to use a smoother with the a formula: log(y+1) ~ log(x
+1).  I'd like to avoid a procedure similar to http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_smooth.html
because it makes exploratory data analysis difficult when I'm
constantly changing factors or facets.  If there's a way to make the
use of models like on the geom_smooth page easily understand changing
factors/facets I'd also be interested in knowing.

I'm still quite new to ggplot2 and R in general so help is very much
appreciated!

# Example:
library(ggplot2)
# Works great
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth
(method="lm", formula= y ~ log(x))

# This smoother is wrong
# geom_smooth draws line the formula without taking the inverse
transormation of the formula (in this case exp(y))
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth
(method="lm", formula= log(y) ~ x)

messages.subject: Re: Highlighing a subset of the data - combining plots
messages.subject_clean: Highlighing a subset of the data - combining plots
messages.body_plain:
On Nov 4, 1:49 pm, Harlan Harris <harlan.har...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I would also add that the "right" way to do this is not to have two
> dataframes, but instead to have a column in your single data frame
> that flags interesting vs noninteresting cases. Then you can do
> something like "+ geom_point(subset=blahblah, color="red")" to overlay
> red dots on the interesting points.

While that is often a useful approach, two dataframes is also a valid
option for annotating a plot (chapter 5.10 of the ggplot2 book). See
also chapter 9, "Manipulating data", on how to subset() an interesting
portion of the data. For example:

library(ggplot2)
# plot engine displacement for each car model
p <- qplot(data=mpg, displ, model, geom="point")
p
# data frame with only the highest engine displacements for each model
highlight <- ddply(mpg, .(model), subset, displ==max(displ))
# red text with number of cylinders for the highlighted subset
p + geom_text(data=highlight, aes(x=displ, y=model, label=cyl),
color="red")

(Note the difference between label=cyl, mapping the label aesthetic to
the cyl variable, and color="red", setting the color of geom_text to a
fixed value. Also note that data is an argument to geom_text, not aes
(). I tend to get confused by this myself.)

Hope this helps,
Jon Olav

> Right, I think where you're getting hung up, Mattias, is a not-
> completely-obvious aspect of how the "+" operator works. When you
> build a ggplot out of a series of calls, what you're actually doing is
> creating a single ggplot object that contains a variety of layers.
> Each plot can only have a single base object, but any number of
> layers. The geom_ and stat_ functions implicitly are adding layers to

> that flags interesting vs noninteresting cases. Then you can do
> something like "+ geom_point(subset=blahblah, color="red")" to overlay
> red dots on the interesting points.
>
> I would further add that summary() of a ggplot object can be helpful
> to see the layers that are generated by your calls. In the future,
> there will likely be a more comprehensive and useful function to do
> this... (work in progress...)
>
>  -Harlan

Hi,

I've recently started with ggplot2 and I have been using it more and
more.
Thanks for such a great library.

I have been using qplot to plot a histogram of a dataframe with the
following command.
d$count holds the frequencies since my data has already been
"tabulated".

qplot(
  d$links,
  data=d,
  weight=d$count,
  geom="histogram",
  binwidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous() +
  scale_y_continuous() +
  labs(x = "links", y = "counts")

Now I have a second dataframe (d2) and would like to use ggplot to
combine two layers in the same plot.
Something like:

ggplot() +
  layer(
    data=d,
    mapping = aes(x=d$links),
    weight=d$count,
    geom="histogram",
    binwidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous() +
  scale_y_continuous() +
  labs(x = "links", y = "counts")

But this isn't working correctly. It seems that weight is not being
set for the histogram.

Thanks in advance for any comments on this issue,
--
Sérgio Nunes

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think you want something like this,

qplot(links, data=d, weight=count, geom="histogram", binwidth = 1) +
  geom_histogram(data=d2, fill="red", binwidth = 1) +

 labs(x = "links", y = "counts")

where geom_histogram() adds a new layer to the plot.

Note that because you specify a data.frame to ggplot or qplot, you
don't need to (and shouldn't) use the $ operator when setting
aesthetics or parameters.

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject_clean: problem with axis labels and facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've been trying to switch to ggplot for the figures in a paper I'm
writing. I'd like to thank Hadley Wickham for the amazing work he did
with this package, it's far superior to lattice in my opinion
(although it does take some getting used to).
I have one figure which is proving troublesome. It has 6 sub-plots,
obtained via faceting, each showing a 2D function as a heat map.
Because they are heat maps, I need the axes to be tight around the
data, otherwise there is some ugly white space around the heat maps.
So I set expand=c(0,0).
Here's the issue: the different heat maps have different (x,y) limits;
so I also need to set scale="free". Unfortunately the axis labels that
appear on the edge of each sub-plots are cut off and I can't seem to
find a way to set different labels in each sub-plot.
Here's a quick illustration of the problem:

dat <- data.frame(x=rep(1:10,2),y=rep(1:10,2),fac=gl(4,5))
qplot(x,y,data=dat) + facet_wrap(~ fac,scales="free") +
scale_x_continuous(breaks=at,expand=c(0,0))

I can always edit the plots later, but it'd be nice to have a work-
around. Thanks for your help!

Simon Barthelmé

Hi Bob,

As far as I can tell all you need to do is add a coordinate transform
to the y-axis, as in:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth

(method="lm", formula= y ~ x) + scale_y_log()

You can check that it's the correct model with:

mtcars$pred <- exp(predict(lm(log(cyl) ~ mpg,dat=mtcars)))
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, cyl)) + geom_point() + scale_y_log() +
geom_smooth(method="lm", formula= y ~ x) + geom_line(aes
(y=pred),col="red")

The red curve overlaps the smoother.

Best,

Simon Barthelme

messages.subject: geom_jitter and %+% subset
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2-ers,

I have data for which I use geom_jitter because answers would otherwise overplot
completely. In a second plot, I want to plot a subset of the data so I can
overlay the two plots in a presentation (building the plot step by step).

"%+%" works very well, except it seems the data of the subset get jittered again
for the second plot, making it look as if these were different data points.

Is there any way to get ggplot2 to only jitter the data once? (I guess an
alternative would be to create extra columns in the data frame that use
jitter(ans1), but it would be nice to do it in the plotting function).

Example:

library(ggplot2)

dat <- data.frame(subject=1:20,ans1=rep(1:4,each=5),ans2=rep(4:1,each=5))
subdat <- subset(dat,ans1>2)

p <- ggplot(dat,aes(x=ans1,y=ans2)) + geom_jitter() + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0.5,4.5)) + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0.5,4.5))

p # full dataset
p %+% subdat  # subset, points are jittered differently

--
Marianne Promberger PhD, King's College London
http://promberger.info
R version 2.10.0 (2009-10-26)
Ubuntu 9.04

messages.subject: Re: custom strip function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It would be nice to be able to re-define panel.background with a
function that is aware of which panel is being drawn (e.g. we could
paint the background with a different colour for each facet, or in
your case add a custom grob at a corner, ...). It's quite easy with
lattice, but I don't see how one would do that with ggplot2.

You could consider creating a geom that works in normalised parent
coordinates as opposed to native,

GeomTest <- proto(Geom, {

  draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ...) {
  with(data,
	gTree(children=gList(
		rectGrob(x,y,default.units="npc",width=1.5*stringWidth(label),height=1.5*stringHeight(label),
		             gp=gpar(fill="grey90"), hjust=hjust,vjust=vjust),
                textGrob(label, unit(x,"npc"), unit(y,"npc"),
default.units="npc", hjust=hjust,vjust=vjust))))

  }

  objname <- "test"

  default_stat <- function(.) StatIdentity
  required_aes <- c("x", "y", "label")
  default_aes <- function(.) aes(hjust=0.5, vjust=0.5)
  guide_geom <- function(x) "blank"

})

geom_test <- GeomTest$build_accessor()

p = qplot(x,y,data=data.frame(x=1:4,y=1:4,f=letters[1:2]), facets=~f)
+ theme_bw()

p + geom_test(aes(label=label), vjust=0, hjust=1,
    data.frame(x=rep(1,2), y=rep(0,2), f=factor(letters[1:2]),
label=LETTERS[1:2]))

HTH,

baptiste

Hi,

GeomTest <- proto(Geom, {

 draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, theme=theme_grey(), ...) {
 with(data, {
   my.label = theme_render(theme, "strip.text.x", label)
   my.label = editGrob(my.label, x= unit(x, "npc"), y = unit(y,
"npc"), hjust=hjust, vjust=vjust)

 guide_geom <- function(x) "blank"

messages.subject: Ordering & stacking variables in bar plots
messages.subject_clean: Ordering & stacking variables in bar plots
messages.body_plain:
Hello group,

I'm having trouble with something I thought would be very simple &
would appreciate some advice!

I want to make some barplots of some ready-summarised data concerning
admission rates to different hospitals. In this simplified example
there are four hospitals and admissions of two types: inpatient (IP) &
day cases (DC).

#Construct example data frame (in wide format to start with)
Hosp = c("Cambridge","Leeds","Birmingham","Southampton")
IP = c(240, 210, 160, 520)
DC = c(1240, 990, 1150, 460)
adm.df = data.frame(Hosp, IP, DC)

#Make basic plot of IP admissions
qplot(Hosp, IP, data = adm.df, geom = "bar")

The first thing I want to do is to order the plot by a variable, e.g.
IP admission rates - this is easy

#Make basic plot of IP admissions ordered by IP admissions
qplot(reorder(Hosp, IP), IP, data = adm.df, geom = "bar")

The next thing I want to do is to stack IP & DC rates in the bar plot
- with the data in wide format this seems tricky - I can plot the sum

#Make plot of the sum of IP + DC
qplot(Hosp, IP + DC, data = adm.df, geom = "bar")

But I don't know if there is any way to make the variables stack
directly from this kind of data frame

Reshaping the data into long format makes it easier

#Reshape data
library(reshape)
madm.df <- melt(adm.df)
names(madm.df) <- c("Hospital","IP_DC","Admissions")

#Now stacking is no trouble
qplot(Hospital, Admissions, data = madm.df, geom = "bar", fill =
IP_DC)

#And ordering the plot by *total* admissions is easy
qplot(reorder(Hospital, Admissions), Admissions, data = madm.df, geom
= "bar", fill = IP_DC)

But how about if I want to go back to ordering the factor Hospital by
just one element of Admissions? e.g. order by just IP admission rates.
This seems hard...

So my two bar plotting questions are:
1) Can I stack two variables from a wide format data frame without
reshaping the data frame first?
2) How can I order a stacked bar plot by just one element in the
stack?

Hope this makes sense

Thanks for any advice!

Andrew Graham
Dept. of Neurology
Addenbrooke's Hospital

Hello

I have been using ggplot2 for the last three months and find it
amazing. However I'm having some problems that I can't seem to find
the solution for.

Essentially half the time I start up R (in Mac) and attempt to use
ggplot, I get the following error message when plotting using wither
ggplot or qplot:

"Error in rename.default(x, .base_to_ggplot) : object '.data' not
found"

All my work is script based, and I know my scripts have worked in the
past. However, I will have to restart R multiple time (and sometimes
the computer) before I can manage to get ggplot to work again. My gut
feeling is that this issue is related to previously restored work
spaces, but I for the life of my can't figure out a correction.

If anyone has any ideas what may be causing this problem, I would love
to hear from you.

Thanks for your time,

David Roth

messages.subject: Re: Ordering & stacking variables in bar plots
messages.subject_clean: Ordering & stacking variables in bar plots
messages.body_plain:
Very clear question! Slightly complex answer...

> So my two bar plotting questions are:
> 1) Can I stack two variables from a wide format data frame without
> reshaping the data frame first?

Nope. ggplot2 likes long-format data frames.

> 2) How can I order a stacked bar plot by just one element in the
> stack?

One way to do it would be to make Hospital an ordered factor, with the
order based on the other variable. Like this (but ideally with better
variable names!):

> x <- subset(madm.df, subset=IP_DC=="IP")
> x[order(x$Admissions), ]
     Hospital IP_DC Admissions
3  Birmingham    IP        160
2       Leeds    IP        210
1   Cambridge    IP        240
4 Southampton    IP        520
> y <- x[order(x$Admissions), ]$Hospital
> y
[1] Birmingham  Leeds       Cambridge   Southampton
Levels: Birmingham Cambridge Leeds Southampton
> madm.df$Hospital <- factor(madm.df$Hospital, levels=y, ordered=TRUE)
> madm.df
     Hospital IP_DC Admissions
1   Cambridge    IP        240
2       Leeds    IP        210
3  Birmingham    IP        160
4 Southampton    IP        520
5   Cambridge    DC       1240
6       Leeds    DC        990
7  Birmingham    DC       1150
8 Southampton    DC        460
> madm.df$Hospital
[1] Cambridge   Leeds       Birmingham  Southampton Cambridge
Leeds
[7] Birmingham  Southampton
Levels: Birmingham < Leeds < Cambridge < Southampton
> ggplot(madm.df, aes(Hospital, Admissions, fill=IP_DC)) + geom_bar(stat="identity")

ggplot is smart enough to know that if your variable is an ordered
factor, you want it plotted in that order.

There may be other ways of doing it, of course...

(I also will add that it's usually easier to understand what's going
on, and to fix problems in your plot, if you use the ggplot syntax
rather than the qplot syntax. Hadley may disagree. :) )

 -Harlan

messages.subject: ggplot2 graphical interface
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley and others

I find this package very nice, and as part of another project have
tried to produce a graphical interface to help  beginners to learn the
syntax is, and explore the layers that are available. The idea is the
following : to use the object structure of the project to display the
default aes and parameters in a graphical interface. When the
aesthetics and parameters and layering have been chosen, then the
graph is displayed along with the formula for that graph. I'm not an
expert programmer but I've tried to produce "a draft" of a package
along that line of thought. It is not finished, and sometimes
especially if you try to build up the layers, the results are weird,
but it should work fine for simple layers.
Before continuing with this program, I would like your opinion.
I've downloaded the package both in zip format and as a tarball in the
documents of this group. It's called ggplot2usr for ggplot2 user
graphical interface. Just install it (it is built for R 2.10), and
then run
library(ggplot2usr)
example(ggplot2usr)
I expect that gtk+ will install when loading gWidgetsRGtk2

Cedric

It seems that qqnorm uses the approach mentioned in: <http://
www.stats.gla.ac.uk/steps/glossary/probability_distributions.html#qqplot <http://www.stats.gla.ac.uk/steps/glossary/probability_distributions.html#qqplot>>.
I found that reference in wikipedia: <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-
Q_plot>.

Here is an excerpt of that webpage:
The quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot is constructed using the theoretical
cumulative distribution function, F(x), of the specified model. The
values in the sample of data, in order from smallest to largest, are
denoted x(1), x(2), ..., x(n). For i = 1, 2, ....., n, x(i) is plotted
against F-1((i-0.5)/n).

Dario

messages.body_plain:
Excellent! Harlan, thank you very much - that's just what I wanted.

It does seem a shame, however, that one has to jump through so many
hoops to solve this. The data frame consists of one factor of four
levels and then eight numbers in two groups of four each - all the
information required to make this plot is explicitly given right there
in the structure of the data frame and the eight values within it.
Presumably (if I had the competence) I could turn your code into a
function to do this ordering for me and then embed it within the call
to ggplot / qplot?

I guess I should develop my R skills and do just that.

Cheers

Andrew

On Nov 14, 3:16 pm, Harlan Harris <harlan.har...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Very clear question! Slightly complex answer...
>
> > So my two bar plotting questions are:
> > 1) Can I stack two variables from a wide format data frame without
> > reshaping the data frame first?
>
> Nope. ggplot2 likes long-format data frames.
>
> > 2) How can I order a stacked bar plot by just one element in the
> > stack?
>
> One way to do it would be to make Hospital an ordered factor, with the
> order based on the other variable. Like this (but ideally with better
> variable names!):
>
> > x <- subset(madm.df, subset=IP_DC=="IP")
> > x[order(x$Admissions), ]
>
>      Hospital IP_DC Admissions
> 3  Birmingham    IP        160
> 2       Leeds    IP        210
> 1   Cambridge    IP        240
> 4 Southampton    IP        520> y <- x[order(x$Admissions), ]$Hospital
> > y
>
> [1] Birmingham  Leeds       Cambridge   Southampton
> Levels: Birmingham Cambridge Leeds Southampton> madm.df$Hospital <- factor(madm.df$Hospital, levels=y, ordered=TRUE)
> > madm.df
>
>      Hospital IP_DC Admissions
> 1   Cambridge    IP        240
> 2       Leeds    IP        210
> 3  Birmingham    IP        160
> 4 Southampton    IP        520
> 5   Cambridge    DC       1240
> 6       Leeds    DC        990
> 7  Birmingham    DC       1150
> 8 Southampton    DC        460> madm.df$Hospital
>
> [1] Cambridge   Leeds       Birmingham  Southampton Cambridge
> Leeds
> [7] Birmingham  Southampton
> Levels: Birmingham < Leeds < Cambridge < Southampton
>
> > ggplot(madm.df, aes(Hospital, Admissions, fill=IP_DC)) + geom_bar(stat="identity")
>
> ggplot is smart enough to know that if your variable is an ordered
> factor, you want it plotted in that order.
>
> There may be other ways of doing it, of course...
>
> (I also will add that it's usually easier to understand what's going
> on, and to fix problems in your plot, if you use the ggplot syntax
> rather than the qplot syntax. Hadley may disagree. :) )
>
>  -Harlan

messages.subject: Re: Re :Re: ggplot2 graphical interface
messages.body_plain:
Cedric,

Thanks for contributing this. I myself am in the formulation stages of
adding ggplot2 graphics in a GUI environment. Though I'm working in
java (see the Deducer package).

As a proof of concept your work is very promising. Here are my initial thoughts:

1. I first had to download gtk+, and could not get it working within
the Mac R Gui, or the terminal. I switched to X11, and had some
success, though I get the message:
(R:1191): Gtk-CRITICAL **: gtk_combo_box_append_text: assertion
`GTK_IS_LIST_STORE (combo_box->priv->model)' failed
upon running the example. Though the functionality seems to work okay.

2. I was able to create a scatter plot very easily, and I liked that
the plotting command was shown in the terminal.

3. I was also able to build layers, adding a smoothed line without
trouble. It is very easy to use from the perspective of someone who
knows ggplot2.

4. The initial ggplot2usr dialog is very general, and provides a
direct mapping of the ggplot2 grammar to the GUI elements. Since this
is a package aimed at beginners, I would also create dialogs
specifically geared towards common types of graphs that they are
interested in. Imagine a person who barely knows what a scatter plot
or histogram is. They may be overwhelmed by the options (i.e. what is
an aes?, what does geom <> stat mean?).

5. Think about the tasks that your users are coming to your system
with. What do they sit down wanting to accomplish? Do they want to
compare two continuous variables? make a histogram? look a the density
of a variable overlayed over a map? Then for each task, write a dialog
that does the task with minimal complexity.

6. The drop down list method of selecting variables becomes very
cumbersome when there are lots of variables. most of the datasets I
work with have more than 300 variables.

7. I've found that dialog memory is very important. If I go from geom
point to smooth, then back again, all the options that I set up are
erased.

8. Also, keep in mind what happens when your windows are resized.

This is a good first effort. I look forward to seeing any subsequent versions.

Cheers,
Ian

> knows ggplot2.

> direct mapping of the ggplot2 grammar to the GUI elements. Since this

> interested in. Imagine a person who barely knows what a scatter plot
> or histogram is. They may be overwhelmed by the options (i.e. what is

messages.subject: Re: Ordering & stacking variables in bar plots
messages.subject_clean: Ordering & stacking variables in bar plots
messages.body_plain:
Great, glad I could help.

I tend to think that ggplot is doing more-or-less the right thing.
Ordering is something that can be done within a data frame, so it's
better to assume that whoever created the data frame knew how they
wanted to order things. So yeah, writing a function to reorder the
factors based on other values sounds like a good plan going forward,
if you're going to be doing this same operation repeatedly!

 -Harlan

On Nov 15, 4:24 pm, Andrew <dr.a.gra...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> Excellent! Harlan, thank you very much - that's just what I wanted.
>
> It does seem a shame, however, that one has to jump through so many
> hoops to solve this. The data frame consists of one factor of four
> levels and then eight numbers in two groups of four each - all the
> information required to make this plot is explicitly given right there
> in the structure of the data frame and the eight values within it.
> Presumably (if I had the competence) I could turn your code into a
> function to do this ordering for me and then embed it within the call
> to ggplot / qplot?
>
> I guess I should develop my R skills and do just that.
>
> Cheers
>
> Andrew
>
> On Nov 14, 3:16 pm, Harlan Harris <harlan.har...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Very clear question! Slightly complex answer...
>
> > > So my two bar plotting questions are:
> > > 1) Can I stack two variables from a wide format data frame without
> > > reshaping the data frame first?
>
> > Nope. ggplot2 likes long-format data frames.
>
> > > 2) How can I order a stacked bar plot by just one element in the
> > > stack?
>
> > One way to do it would be to make Hospital an ordered factor, with the
> > order based on the other variable. Like this (but ideally with better
> > variable names!):
>
> > > x <- subset(madm.df, subset=IP_DC=="IP")
> > > x[order(x$Admissions), ]
>
> >      Hospital IP_DC Admissions
> > 3  Birmingham    IP        160
> > 2       Leeds    IP        210
> > 1   Cambridge    IP        240
> > 4 Southampton    IP        520> y <- x[order(x$Admissions), ]$Hospital
> > > y
>
> > [1] Birmingham  Leeds       Cambridge   Southampton
> > Levels: Birmingham Cambridge Leeds Southampton> madm.df$Hospital <- factor(madm.df$Hospital, levels=y, ordered=TRUE)
> > > madm.df
>
> >      Hospital IP_DC Admissions
> > 1   Cambridge    IP        240
> > 2       Leeds    IP        210
> > 3  Birmingham    IP        160
> > 4 Southampton    IP        520
> > 5   Cambridge    DC       1240
> > 6       Leeds    DC        990
> > 7  Birmingham    DC       1150
> > 8 Southampton    DC        460> madm.df$Hospital
>
> > [1] Cambridge   Leeds       Birmingham  Southampton Cambridge
> > Leeds
> > [7] Birmingham  Southampton
> > Levels: Birmingham < Leeds < Cambridge < Southampton
>
> > > ggplot(madm.df, aes(Hospital, Admissions, fill=IP_DC)) + geom_bar(stat="identity")
>
> > ggplot is smart enough to know that if your variable is an ordered
> > factor, you want it plotted in that order.
>
> > There may be other ways of doing it, of course...
>
> > (I also will add that it's usually easier to understand what's going
> > on, and to fix problems in your plot, if you use the ggplot syntax
> > rather than the qplot syntax. Hadley may disagree. :) )
>
> >  -Harlan

messages.subject: using geom_rect()
messages.body_plain:
Hi - I'm new to ggplot2 and am trying to annotate some time series
plots with ablines and/or colored polygons. I've been trying to follow
examples from the book (pages 85-97), but am not getting it dialed in.

Here's what I've tried. The data look like this:
> head(turtle11[,1:8])
     long     lat track       date   an.lat   an.long    sst chl
1 8573451 2048370    11 1997-01-23 18.11202 -102.8971     NA   0
2 8575219 2047292    11 1997-01-24 18.10281 -102.8812 27.675   0
3 8574096 2047592    11 1997-01-25 18.10537 -102.8913 27.675   0
4 8571694 2046170    11 1997-01-26 18.09322 -102.9129 27.750   0
5 8570149 2048441    11 1997-01-27 18.11263 -102.9268     NA   0
6 8571539 2040865    11 1997-01-28 18.04786 -102.9143 27.750   0

yrng <- range(turtle11$chl,na.rm=T)
chl  <- ggplot(turtle11,aes(date,chl))
chl  <- chl + layer(geom="path")
chl  <- chl + xlab("Date") + ylab("Chlorophyll A")
chl

This works fine. But then this effort to put in an abline fails:

chl <- chl + geom_vline(aes(xintercept=as.Date("1997-09-01")))
chl

> chl
Error in data.frame(xintercept = 10105, x = c(9884, 9885, 9886,
9887,  :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 1, 481

Similarly, my two efforts to make a rectangle fail as well:
1)
> chl <- chl + geom_rect(aes(xmin=range(turtle11$date)[1],xmax=as.Date("1997-09-01"),ymin=yrng[1],ymax=yrng[2]))
> chl
Error in data.frame(xintercept = 10105, x = c(9884, 9885, 9886,
9887,  :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 1, 481

2)
> noswfs <- data.frame(
+ 	x=c(range(turtle11$date)[1],as.Date("1997-09-01")),
+ 	y=range(turtle11$chl,na.rm=T)
+ )
>
> chl <- chl + geom_rect(aes(NULL,NULL,xmin=noswfs$x[1],xmax=noswfs$x[2],ymin=noswfs$y[1],ymax=noswfs$y[2]),data=noswfs)
> chl
Error in data.frame(xintercept = 10105, x = c(9884, 9885, 9886,
9887,  :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 1, 481

Thanks in advance for any advice,
Rob

messages.subject: Drawing a series of ggplots in multiple windows
messages.subject_clean: Drawing a series of ggplots in multiple windows
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using ggplot to examine variable distributions per subject in a
dataset containing ~70 people. Using geom_boxplot with flipped
coordinates and 70 folks makes for very tiny boxplots, so my thought
was to break things down into graphs of 10 people per graph, creating
a new graphics window for each plot. But when I call dev.new <http://dev.new> and
ggplot within a loop, nothing is graphed on R 2.10.0 on Windows 7.
Here is a minimally reproducible example:

exampleData <- data.frame(id=rep(1:30, each=24), congruence=rep(rep
(1:3, each=8), 30), reactionTime=rnorm(720, mean=10, sd=2))
numplots <- ceiling(length(unique(exampleData$id))/10)
idList <- unique(exampleData$id)
for (i in 1:numplots) {
  workingIds <- idList[((i-1)*10+1):min((i*10), length(idList))]
  workingSubset <- exampleData[exampleData$id %in% workingIds,]
  dev.new <http://dev.new>()
  ggplot(workingSubset, aes(x=factor(id), y=reactionTime)) +
geom_boxplot() + coord_flip() + facet_grid(. ~ congruence)
#  plot(workingSubset$id, workingSubset$reactionTime)
}

Note that the ggplot command works perfectly when executed outside of
the loop. And when I use a base graphics function, such as the plot
command commented out above, I also receive one plot per window, as
expected. So my hunch is that ggplot is failing to link with the
graphics device I've created, but I'm not sure how to fix this
problem.

Thanks for your help!

Michael

messages.subject: extension of facet_grid? facet_array? tricks?
messages.body_plain:
Before asking for advice let me say 2 quick things:

1) I'm fairly new to R and ggplot2, but I'm very excited about
ggplot2. Just using facet_grid has changed my life, not to mention
learning the grammar.

2) There was an older post enquiring about extending facet_grid (or
facet_wrap) beyond its current capabilities. (there were no replies).
I'm wondering about this too, but I'm also suspecting that if I were
clever enough, I might be able to get some of the functionality i'm
looking for. I didnt see any other older posts on this topic.

I'm using facet_grid to show the results for 3 different statistics
at, say, 4 levels of modeling resolution, that is stats~level. So the
grid is 4x3. Within each facet/subplot, there are 4 models on the x
axis and their score on the y. Furthermore, above each model tick
there are 4 jittered points with colors showing results for 4
different model setups. THat's awesome and easy in ggplot2!

All of the above conveniently summarizes data at 1 location. But I
have 6 locations, which is another faceting dimension, if you will.
But I find myself having exhausted facet_grid. Maybe I could do
something like facet_wrap(~(stats~level)) but I'm assuming that wont
work.

What I'm currently doing is using viewport and looping over the
data.frame, subsetting on location in each iteration and plotting to
the desired location in the multi-plot output. This actually works
well, and is kind of an adhoc facet_array or facet_matrix. The only
unsavory thing is the unnecessary repetition of the color legend. If
this were a true "facet_array" it would just plot that once in a
easily manageable way.

What I'm grappling with and looking for advice on is the best way to
banish the multiple color legends and efficiently get one legend in a
nice place while using viewport, or any other way that would work.

Thanks,

James

previously saved workspaces. This solution is for the Mac version of R
(and the problem may be unique to the mac version as well).

problems since.

mv ~/.RData ~/workspace.RData
mv ~/.Rhistory ~/history.txt

Dave Roth

messages.subject: Re: extension of facet_grid? facet_array? tricks?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kasper,

thanks, this is a step in the right direction. It appears that going
this route, so that the plot is laid out nicely, involves using
viewport in a detailed fashion. My first reading of viewport was
somewhat opaque, but I'll mess with it. If someone can illustrate a
proper way to do this with the code I've now provided below, I'd be
grateful.

Re the code below, there was a post which seems to have evaporated,
asking for some reproducible code. I shied away from this in my first
post, since it seemed like a lot of details, but I've now provided it
below. You should just be able to run it to see what i'm complaining
about, the repeated legends that I have to wrestle with. The second
plot, shows removal of all legends. I havent shown plotting only the
legend as Kaspar suggested, but it does omit the plot and put the
legend where it would have been with the plot present, at least using
the snytax of the previous post.

To me, resorting to witholding legends/plots and using view port is
less than ideal because its conjuring memories of some of the things I
hoped ggplot would cure. This is what I was alluding to when I wrote
the nonsense syntax facet_wrap(~(stats~level))  i wasnt being careful
here. More precisely, it should have been something more like
facet_grid(site~(stats~level)), since ggplot would need to know what
variables to be subsetting on at each level. This is essentially what
I have achieved by doing the subsetting in the loop (over ss below),
only I'm forced to fuss with legends which is so un-ggplot2. To me it
makes sense to want to extend the idea of facet_grid to more
dimensions. I think some could argue for using the formula syntax to
get at some of this, but i havent been sucessful with this and it
seems like it would tend to clutter more than simplify the
presentation.

cheers,
James

---------------------------------------
require(ggplot2)

#set up the data frame
len=243 #=3^5
data=data.frame(value=rnorm(len))
data$setup=factor( c(rep('setup1',len/3),rep('setup2',len/3),rep
('setup3',len/3)) )
data$site=factor( rep (c(rep('site1',len/9),rep('site2',len/9),rep
('site3',len/9)), 3) )
data$level=factor( rep( c(rep('lev1',len/27),rep('lev2',len/27),rep
('lev3',len/27)),9 ))
data$model=factor( rep( c(rep('mod1',len/81),rep('mod2',len/81),rep
('mod3',len/81)),27 ))
data$stat=factor( rep( c('stat1','stat2','stat3'),81 ) )

# will need this for subsetting
sites=unique(data$site)

# need this for viewporting
vplayout<-function(x,y) viewport(layout.pos.row=x,layout.pos.col=y)

#some plot option values
grid.line.type='solid'
grid.line.size=.2
model.name.size=6

# first plot, showing multiple, repeated, unnecessary legends
x11(h=6,w=15)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(1,3)))
for (ss in 1:length(sites)) {
  site=sites[ss]
  plot <-
    ggplot( data[which(data$site==site),],
           aes(model,value,shape=setup)) +
             geom_jitter()+
               facet_grid(level~stat)+
                 theme_bw() +
                   opts(axis.text.x=theme_text
(size=model.name.size,hjust=1,angle=90),
                        panel.grid.major= theme_line
(linetype=grid.line.type,
                          colour='gray50',size=grid.line.size),
title=site)
  print(plot , vp=vplayout(((ss-1) %/% 3)+1,((ss-1) %% 3)+1))
}

## this is removing the legends, all of them....
x11(h=6,w=15)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(1,3)))
for (ss in 1:length(sites)) {
  site=sites[ss]
  plot <-
    ggplot( data[which(data$site==site),],
           aes(model,value,shape=setup)) +
             geom_jitter()+
               facet_grid(level~stat) +
                 theme_bw() +
                   opts(axis.text.x=theme_text
(size=model.name.size,hjust=1,angle=90),
                        panel.grid.major= theme_line
(linetype=grid.line.type,
                          colour='gray50',size=grid.line.size),
title=site,
                        legend.position='none')
  print(plot , vp=vplayout(((ss-1) %/% 3)+1,((ss-1) %% 3)+1))
}

Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
A 2nd Y axis is not yet a feature of ggplot. Hadley did promise that he was going to think about this over Christmas, exactly for the situation
where the same underlying construct was being measured on both the axes... but denominated differently.   I do not think that Hadley intends to write anything that would like some Y variables to one axis and other Y variables to another axis.

I  suppose, with apologies to Tolkien, the stance could be paraphrased:

One axis  to rule them all,
 One axis  to find them,
 One axis  to bring them all...

R

messages.subject: Re: extension of facet_grid? facet_array? tricks?
messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

I agree that it's frustrating to have to do it yourself for more
complicated facetting examples like the attached.  However, it's very
difficult to design a system that works more generally.  For example,
how would your proposed syntax work if you wanted facet_wrap nested
inside facet_grid?  Should you allow a fixed amount of nesting, or an
unlimited amount, so you could have facet_wrap nested inside
facet_grid nested inside facet_wrap?  How would you deal with free
scales?  To start with, what sorts of restrictions would you even want
to apply?  If you wanted manually specified limits that vary across
facets, how would you describe them?  (I haven't even figured out how
to do this for the simpler cases that currently exist).

Then once you've figured out the basic syntax and structure, you have
to write all the drawing code, dealing with the various possibilities
for axis positions.  And then you have to document it all.  It's a lot
of work for a feature that will only be used by a few people,
especially when there is already a way to work around it.

That's not to say I'd never implement it, because I like the elegance
of having a fully recursive facetting specification, but it's pretty
unlikely unless I have some insight into a nice way to represent all
the possibilities.

Hadley

> original data frame ?

Yes:

qplot( month, tau, data = top10, geom = "line", colour = "top10" ) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = "top100") data = top100, linetype = "dashed" )

but it's a bit easier to see what's going on if you use ggplot()

ggplot(aes(month, tau)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = "top10"), data = top10) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = "top100"), data = top100)

messages.subject: Re: extension of facet_grid? facet_array? tricks?
messages.body_plain:
On Nov 19, 6:29 pm, McCreight <mccre...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Re the code below, there was a post which seems to have evaporated,

Yeah, I used the "Reply to author" option in Google groups. Nice to
hear that you got it; I never see those messages again myself 8-)

> asking for some reproducible code. I shied away from this in my first
> post, since it seemed like a lot of details, but I've now provided it
> below.

Thanks! If I understand correctly, this gives what you want except for
splitting on "site":
qplot(data=data, model, value, shape=setup, facets=level~stat)

or for the hardcore ggplotter:
ggplot(data, aes(model, value, shape=setup)) + facet_grid(level~stat)
+ geom_point()

(or you could use colour=setup to match the image you posted
here...mind the u, "color" won't work as of ggplot2 0.8.3)).

I _think_ you're supposed to be able to use facets=level~site+stat:
qplot(data=data, model, value, shape=setup, facets=level~site+stat)

However, the corresponding example (search for ". ~ vs + am") at
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/facet_grid.html
is currently broken. (Faceting on multiple row (or column) variables
is also described in the "facet grid" section of the "positioning"
chapter of the ggplot2 book, so I guess it _is_ intended to work.)

A crude workaround is
data$sitestat <- with(data, interaction(site, stat))
qplot(data=data, model, value, shape=setup, facets=level~sitestat)

This gives you a quick overview, though with clumsy column headers and
without nice gaps between sites. On the other hand, if I needed a plot
for publication now, I'd just loop over levels of "site", make
separate plots, crop away the unnecessary legends, and combine the
plots outside of R. Hopefully, faceting on multiple row (or column)
variables will be fixed in a future version.

Hope this helps,
Jon Olav

This is how I deal to convert a regular grid (polygons) into a dataframe

grelhaOrd <- data.frame("Id"=as.numeric(row.names(grelha@data)),"Quad"=grelha@data[,1])

#! === Converter SpatialPolygonDF em Dataframe para gráficos ggplot2
grelhamap <- lapply(slot(grelha, "polygons"), function(x) lapply(slot(x, "Polygons"), function(y) slot(y, "coords"))) #! Converte SPDF em List
dfTmp <- list()
for (i in 1:dim(summary(grelhamap))[1])
{
  dfTmp[[i]] <- data.frame(grelhamap[i],"Id"=i-1,"Ordem"=seq(1:5))  #! adiciona o código e a ordem das coordenadas à cada linha
}
dfGrid <- do.call(rbind,dfTmp) #! Obtem-se um Dataframe para o ggplot2 a partir do objecto List
dfGrid <- merge(dfGrid,grelhaOrd,by="Id")

Paulo

messages.subject: Re: Weighting question
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Nov 21, 2009 at 5:16 PM, AC Del Re <acd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi ggplotters,
> I am attempting to place a weighted regression line on a scatterplot and and
> have come up with 2 possible solutions. Based on the code, it seems like
> both should result in the identical placements of the intercept and slope
> but they are different (intercept varies). Not sure what is going on but
> help in understanding this is appreciated. The syntax for both graphs are
> below along with attachments of the two outputs.
> #graph 1
> gg.reg1 <- lm(del ~ n.sess, weights=wt.del) #weighting in regression
> lm_smooth<-geom_smooth(method=lm,size=1,data= gg.reg1,se=FALSE)
> qplot(n.sess,del,data=grief2, size=wt.del)+lm_smooth

This specification doesn't make that much sense - you're taking
gg.reg1 which ggplot converts into a data frame of explanatory
variables and predictors and then fits a smooth line to - i.e. you're
fitting a linear model to the output of a linear model.  I think you
want:

qplot(n.sess,del,data=grief2, weight=wt.del,size=wt.del)+
geom_smooth(method = lm, se = F)

Hadley

--

Hi,

If a fully recursive facetting specification is difficult to conceive,
maybe a good workaround could be a more flexible way to arrange
several ggplots in a page. For example, latticeExtra provides a
c.trellis method whereby two plots can be combined into one with some
parameters in common (e.g. one axis, the legend, etc.).

This requires full control over the size of the different viewports of
ggplot (making sure the panels are aligned and have the same size),
which I don't think we have at the moment. I imagine the following
typical example,

p1 = qplot(...)
p2 = qplot(...)

p12 = arrange(p1, p2, ncol=2, common.yaxis = FALSE,
                    common.legend=TRUE, legend.position="right")

This could obviously become more complicated when the plots have
facets (do we try to align all the panels? -- probably not), but at
least some of the options could remain available (legend, layout,
title, theme, etc.).

The main problem with implementing this currently is that if you
remove an element of a ggplot, such as the legend, it resizes itself
to fill the viewport. Also, if you want to plot only a legend, its
size is rather bizarre (e.g. I failed in calculating its grobWidth in
absolute units), which makes it difficult to control the layout of
several plots accurately.

Just a thought anyway,

All the best,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: new ggplot2 web application
messages.body_plain:
Very slick. This is fantastic work. It feels smooth and easy. The
enumeration of the options through the menu system give the user a
good idea of what options are available, whereas you need to go to the
docs in the command line. I know how hard it is to make a nice
interface, and yours is quite elegant.

Two minor points:
1. When editing the layer options, one has to navigate through 4
levels of contextual menus. If I need to change a couple options for a
single layer (as you did in your demo) I need to travel through this
deep structure multiple times.

2. When I right click on the x/y labels or the legend I expected to be
able to edit them.

One major point:
1. I know everyone has their own opinions about how they like to
interface with their software, but the biggest limitation for me is
that this is locked up in a web app. I (and everyone I know) do all my
data manipulation and analysis on a local machine. To then have to
write it out to a local file and load it to the web (unencrypted) is
simply not going to happen for me. Perhaps an SPSS / non-R user would
be more inclined to do so because of limitations in SPSS.

Cheers,
Ian

p.s. How have we not met? I think I'm down the hall from you (in the
first year PhD office). Drop me a line...

proportional to 1/var(effect size), which is the weighting factor for

give an idea of the range of values represented by point size.

when a similar explanation as above is given. The legend values

circle points in the legend key do not match up with the shapes in the
graph. Do others see this legend being unnecessary and somewhat
confusing?

messages.subject: Re: Greys
messages.body_plain:
I wonder whether trying to get it right for all circumstances is the
best approach; projectors and screens vary so much.  I wonder if it
might be possible to have a "test pattern" which one could throw up on
one's 'best guess' projector/printer and then choose the limit value
that way.  ie. have a function that prints out a test PDF, then read
off a code from that, then feed that code to set_theme() for actually
producing graphs.

Of course in some situations you're just dealing with such terrible
contrast that knowing ahead of time that you're limited to four of
five gradients that can be reliably distinguished; that sucks but
knowing it ahead of time is better than finding out during your
presentation.

messages.subject_clean: map_data objects are no longer spatial objects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Without projecting the data latitude and longitude are coordinates on a
sphere.
In the spirit of separating the data from the plot, one should project
prior to plotting.
In general for maps an aspect ratio of 1 is appropriate. Let the
projection
handle the stretching. So if you want to plot the world flat, you need
to project
it first.

Nicholas

messages.subject: Re: map_data objects are no longer spatial objects?
messages.subject_clean: map_data objects are no longer spatial objects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hardley,

This is something to think about. I don't know how ggplot2 manage to
plot cartesian coordinates or what is happening when we set a coord_map
().

We'd need to know how ggplot2 deals generally with the relation
between plot region/aspect ratio.

There are a lot of considerations about this issue. I agree that
projecting data should precede plotting. In doing so, coordinates
should no longer be presented in degrees as default, as some examples
of coord_maps. For New Zealand for example there is no mention to wich
Datum is being used, NZGD49, NZG200 or WGS84. The geocentric Datum
should always be refered for unprojected data; possibly GRS80,
although differences between NZG2000 and GRS80 (or WGS84) are
negligible. When presenting projected data, the Lat long grid  shown
is meaningless, as I understand it. New Zealand Mercator projection
Grid could be printed instead. Did you crossed your outputs with GIS
ones?
Maps shown at coord_maps are beautiful but lacks the desired spatial
integrity and coherent scaling.

Back to proportions and aspect ratio, Can't the approach be the same
used when plotting a SPDF?

Something interesting to explore.

Paulo

messages.subject: Re: x axis label and prediction curve
messages.subject_clean: x axis label and prediction curve
messages.body_plain:
Hi Maarten,
I'm not sure about extrapolating the prediction curve. I think you could do it by hand with predict, assuming the method exists for the model you are using. And then ploting it as another layer.
What I'm sure is that you have to use expression to use the square root symbol. See ?plotmath for more. The code for that is:

#I'm assuming your x axis is of a continous variable, otherwise square-rooting it would make much sense, would it?
p+scale_x_continuous(expression(sqrt("your_var")))

Sorry I couldn't be of more help
Luciano

messages.body_plain:
Just an exercise

I reproduced some of the examples presented at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/coord_map.html in a GIS. Plots presented are, in some cases, quite different from expected, as you can see from attached PDF.
This is relevant for anyone interested in presenting cartographic maps via ggplot.

Paulo

2009/11/25 Paulo Eduardo Cardoso <pauloed...@gmail.com>

> Hi Hardley,
>
> This is something to think about. I don't know how ggplot2 manage to
> plot cartesian coordinates or what is happening when we set a coord_map
> ().
>
> We'd need to know how ggplot2 deals generally with the relation
> between plot region/aspect ratio.
>
> There are a lot of considerations about this issue. I agree that
> projecting data should precede plotting. In doing so, coordinates
> should no longer be presented in degrees as default, as some examples
> of coord_maps. For New Zealand for example there is no mention to wich
> Datum is being used, NZGD49, NZG200 or WGS84. The geocentric Datum
> should always be refered for unprojected data; possibly GRS80,
> although differences between NZG2000 and GRS80 (or WGS84) are
> negligible. When presenting projected data, the Lat long grid  shown
> is meaningless, as I understand it. New Zealand Mercator projection
> Grid could be printed instead. Did you crossed your outputs with GIS
> ones?
> Maps shown at coord_maps are beautiful but lacks the desired spatial
> integrity and coherent scaling.
>
>
> Back to proportions and aspect ratio, Can't the approach be the same
> used when plotting a SPDF?

>
>

It is always a good idea to give a reproducible example wich includes
some sample data.

> And now I want to add on top of this filled density plot several other
> density plots, not in a filled fashion but as lines (these additional
> densityplots were subsamples from the entire population).

like this?

sampdat <- data.frame(SampScheme=c("population","one","two"),DEM=rnorm(3000))

m <- ggplot(sampdat[sampdat$SampScheme=="population",], aes(x=DEM))

m <- m + geom_density(colour="darkgreen",size=2, fill="green")
m + geom_density(data=sampdat[sampdat$SampScheme!="population",],aes(colour=SampScheme))

best regards,
 stefan

Dear Joe,

Reformat your data. That will make things much easier. Here is an example with a good structure but with dummy data.

ed.data <- expand.grid(Proficiency.Level =
1:4, Subject = c("math", "reading"), type = c("504.0", "504.1", "sped"))

ed.data
$pointestimate <- rnorm(nrow(ed.data)) + ed.data$Proficiency.Level

ed.data
$LCL <- ed.data$pointestimate - 1.96

ed.data
$UCL <- ed.data$pointestimate + 1.96

ggplot(subset(ed.data, type
== "sped"), aes(x = Proficiency.Level, y = pointestimate, ymin = LCL, ymax = UCL, colour = Subject)) + geom_ribbon(fill="gray",alpha=.25,lwd=.5) + geom_point()

HTH,

Thierry

messages.subject: RE: multiple dataset plot error
messages.body_plain:
Try

ggplot(v, aes(x = dist, y = gamma)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(data = vmf.line)

Or since vmf.line is probably the modelled variogram

ggplot(v, aes(x = dist, y = gamma)) + geom_point() + geom_line(data = vmf.line)

Something I tend to do with empirical variogram data

ggplot(v, aes(x = dist, y = gamma)) + geom_smooth(weights = np / dist ^ 2) + geom_point()

HTH,

Thierry

> PS Hadley, can we write methods (S3 or S4) so that ggplot does something like the
> code below when v is a variogram object? In this case ggplot(v) could be sufficient
> information for a method. As a variogram object always uses the same variable names.

See the section "ggplot methods" in the book:

ggplot() is a generic function, with different methods for different
types of data. The most common input, and what we have used until now,
is a data frame. As with base and lattice graphics, it is possible to
extend ggplot() to work with other types of data. However, the way
this works with \ggplot is fundamentally different: ggplot2 will not
give you a complete plot, but instead will give you the tools you need
to make any plot you desire.

Hadley

messages.subject: Label reordering in color scales?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

I just noticed something when using scale_colour_identity which I had assumed worked before, but appears not only to not work in scale_colour_identity, but also in the more basic scale_colour_discrete, so I assume it doesn't work in general.

The quirk comes when you give the labeler (or, I suppose, any other argument as well) a named vector and expect the scaling function to check the labels with the data values.   Here's an example :

df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10, z = factor(rep(1:2, each = 5)))

ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = z), data = df) +
  geom_point()

ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = z), data = df) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_discrete(labels = c('1' = 'One', '2' = 'Two'))

ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = z), data = df) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_discrete(labels = c('2' = 'Two', '1' = 'One'))

While no warning or error flags the mislabeling, the fact that you are giving scale_colour_discrete the named vector doesn't seem to matter; what matters is the order.

Strangely enough, if you play with the values, Hadley gives an example under http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/scale_manual.html which does work correctly (which led me to believe it worked for other arguments as well) :

p <- qplot(mpg, wt, data = mtcars, colour = factor(cyl))
p
p + scale_colour_manual(values = c('6' = 'green', '8' = 'red', '4' = 'blue'))
p + scale_colour_manual(values = c('8' = 'red', '6' = 'green', '4' = 'blue'))

However, you can check that you get the same problem as before if you play with the labels instead of the values.  Does anyone know of a general rule as to when ggplot2 will recognize the named vectors or won't?  Is there a workaround?  I'm sure there's some easy thing I'm just missing here...

Cheers - thanks for the help
david.

messages.subject: an interesting example of facets
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to point to an interesting example using facets and ask how
one might do something similar in ggplot2.

The example is from Charles Franklin at pollster.com <http://pollster.com> who does a lot of
interesting charts (using R).  See http://www.pollster.com/blogs/unemployment_trends_in_the_sta.php

He's showing unemployment rates for each of the states so he is really
pushing hard to use limited space as effectively as possible. I like
the fact that he used the spots in the facet grid for something other
than one of the small multiples.  In one he puts a scale (so he can
avoid taking the space elsewhere) and in another he has information
about the source of the data.

I can imagine how one might do this in lattice, short of using grid
graphics to manually assemble the facets one by one, I don't know how
one would do it in ggplot2. Or maybe it's straightforward to get the
matrix of grid objects that make up the facets in a ggplot2 facet
grid.

Please don't take this as a criticism of ggplot2. I rely on it very
much and I am just thinking about how to use it to flatter Charles
Franklin by trying to imitate him.

messages.subject: Re: Misplaced xlab and use of annote()
messages.subject_clean: Misplaced xlab and use of annote()
messages.body_plain:
The extra white space is a consequence of opts(aspect.ration=1), and
it's possible that you'll have to wait until Hadley finishes the
layout update to get a true fix, in the meantime, here's a hacked
solution:

ctrl <- read.table('Control.txt', header = TRUE)
tail <- read.table('tail.txt', header = TRUE)
peak <- read.table('Peak.txt', header = TRUE)
noch <- read.table('noChange.txt', header = TRUE)
require(ggplot2)
lo.peak <- loess(y ~ x, data = peak)
loPred.peak <- predict(lo.peak, data.frame(x = 14:73), se = FALSE)
lo.noch <- loess(y ~ x, noch)
loPred.noch <- predict(lo.noch, data.frame(x = 0:47), se = FALSE)
lo.ctrl <- loess(y ~ x, ctrl)
loPred.ctrl <- predict(lo.ctrl, data.frame(x = 13:47), se = FALSE)
lo.tail <- loess(y ~ x, tail)
loPred.tail <- predict(lo.tail, data.frame(x = 12:55), se = FALSE)
bg <- data.frame(time = 0:72, peak = NA, tail = NA, ctrl = NA, noch = NA)
bg$peak[14:73] <- loPred.peak
bg$noch[1:48] <- loPred.noch
bg$ctrl[13:47] <- loPred.ctrl
bg$tail[12:55] <- loPred.tail
bg.s <- with(bg, data.frame(time = rep(time, 4), stack(bg, select = -time)))

bg.note = ddply(
	.data = bg.s
	, .variables = .(ind)
	, .fun = function(x){
		x = x[!is.na <http://is.na>(x$value),]
		x = x[order(x$time),]
		x = x[nrow(x),]
		labels = c('7.94','7.00','6.98','6.02')
		x$label = labels[x$ind==c("peak", "noch", "ctrl", "tail")]
		return(x)
	}
)
p <- qplot(time, values, colour = ind, data = bg.s, geom = 'line',
       xlab = 'time (s)\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n', ylab = 'momentary
affective responses')
p <- p + scale_colour_hue('ad type (liking)',
       breaks = c("peak", "noch", "ctrl", "tail"),
       labels = c("positive added (7.94)", "neutral precedes (7.00)",
"control (6.98)", "neutral added (6.02)"))
p <- p + opts(aspect.ratio = 1)
p <- p + geom_text(
	data = bg.note
	, mapping = aes(
		label = label
	)
	, hjust=0
	, legend = FALSE
)
p <- p + scale_x_continuous(
	limits = c(0,80)
)
ggsave(p,file='BaumgartnerEtAl1977-Figure1.pdf')
print(p)

messages.subject: Facet labels when using facet_wrap()
messages.body_plain:
Dear Group,

I have some plotmath expressions I'd like to use as the facet labels.
I've got this all working with facet_grid(), but I'm getting the
following error with facet_wrap():

> p <- ggplot(scrs, aes(PC1, PC2, size = abundance, shape = cluster)) +
+     xlab("PC1") + ylab("PC2") +
+     facet_wrap(. ~ species, labeller = "label_parsed")
Error in get("new", env = FacetWrap, inherits = TRUE)
(FacetWrap, ...) :
  unused argument(s) (labeller = "label_parsed")

This suggests facet_wrap() isn't able to handle the labeller argument.

I want to use facet_wrap as I only have a 1-d variable but want the
facets laid out on a grid to save space.

Here's a reproducible example:

set.seed(123)
spps <- factor(paste("species", sample(1:3, 10, replace = TRUE)),
               levels = paste("species", 1:3),
               labels = c(expression(italic(species ~ 1)),
               expression(italic(species ~ 2)),
               expression(italic(species ~ 3))))
DF <- data.frame(PC1 = rnorm(10), PC2 = rnorm(10),
                 abundance = runif(10),
                 species = spps,
                 cluster = factor(sample(1:3, 10, replace = TRUE)))
p <- ggplot(DF, aes(PC1, PC2, size = abundance, shape = cluster)) +
    xlab("PC1") + ylab("PC2") +
    facet_wrap(~ species, labeller = "label_parsed")
p + geom_point()

If this isn't possible, can someone suggest a work around with
facet.grid such that I can specify a new variable so I get the 3 plots
on a 2x2 grid (there will be one empty panel, lower right)

TIA

G

--

messages.subject: how to best deal with overplotting
messages.subject_clean: how to best deal with overplotting
messages.body_plain:
All,

    I know that there are several different ways to deal with
overplotting with ggplot 2, but none of them seem to capture what I am
looking for, when "the rubber hits the road".  My problem is as
follows:

1) I have data across 2 dimensions, x & y, with one legend already
consumed by a categorical factor
2) I have data that will span several orders of magnitude, sometimes
with sparse data, and sometimes with dense data.

    What I am "normally" used to doing is to perform an x-y "point"
plot with different colors to represent the different categories, then
I will place a histogram below the x-axis and to the left of the y-
axis (broken down by factor in each case).  I cannot seem to find a
nice, easy way to create a histogram inside of the plot.  It can be
done, but not easily at all, to my knowledge / skill level.

    I have tried the following methods:
  o  point plot, making the points smaller, turning on a little
jitter, and giving some alpha.  I don't like this because (a) I REALLY
have to make the points tiny to make data points not pile on top of
each other which makes the sparse points hard to see, (b) I don't like
jitter because it is distorting the data, and (c) alpha similarly
makes certain points disappear.
  o  bin_2d plot, with the colour as the factor and the fill as
the ..count..  I don't like this because a particular bin is EITHER
one factor or the other, so a lot of data is lost.  Plus, when I put
in two "aes" parameters like ..count.. and my factor, the legend for
count becomes empty.  I could probably figure out what I am doing
wrong in that, though.
  o  I have also created a point plot like above, but with an overlay
of "stat_density2d", using "tile" and fill by density, to create an
effect similar to what Hadley has in his example.  I then put a low
alpha on this plot so that it is mostly see-through and I can see the
points behind it.  But again, this ends up making the graph just not-
quite-right.  The density layer really just darkens things and it is
hard to see the variation in density.

    Barring a solution that would relatively easily be able to create
a histogram, which would be ideal, the easiest other solution that I
see is to plot the points in a different ORDER.  E.g., if I have 3
factors, A, B, and C, I would like to be able to plot so that A is
drawn first, then B, then C.  Then draw the plot again so that C is
drawn first, then A, etc.  In this manner, I can use multiple plots of
the same data set so that I can see how many points of the "other
factor" are hidden behind the factor that is being drawn last.  I am
hoping this is feasible in it.  Otherwise, I'll have to go back to non-
ggplot plots, and draw the data one factor at a time.

                                              Thanks!
                                                      Mike Williamson
